prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: GCS 9 and a severe immunocompromised state (CD4 68) are imaging-first criteria under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
Do not treat with the community-acquired regimen (ceftriaxone with or without vancomycin) empirically: this is hospital-acquired Gram-negative meningitis on hospital day 18.
Do not attribute the obtundation to sepsis-associated encephalopathy or hyponatraemia without examining the CSF.
required_recommendations: Give vancomycin plus meropenem 2 g IV within 60 minutes, after cultures (IDSA 2017): the first dose in full, then an interval set by creatinine clearance, about 43 mL/min by Cockcroft-Gault at 44 kg and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, which gives meropenem 2 g every 12 hours; review it daily, since dolutegravir and trimethoprim raise serum creatinine without lowering GFR.
Remove or replace the urinary catheter as soon as antibiotics have started.

Adjunctive dexamethasone is not indicated once Gram-negative bacillary healthcare-associated meningitis is established: it has no established benefit here (IDSA 2017), and with CD4 68, cryptococcal antigenaemia and recently treated tuberculous meningitis it adds risk.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because GCS is 9 and she is severely immunocompromised (advanced HIV, CD4 68) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP, and on the same specimen exclude tuberculous meningitis relapse and cryptococcal meningitis in parallel: AFB stain, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, mycobacterial culture and a repeat CSF cryptococcal antigen rather than the earlier negative result; these must not delay Gram-negative therapy.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: Proteus mirabilis susceptible to ceftriaxone and meropenem and resistant to ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; stop vancomycin and continue meropenem or step to ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours.

Start fluconazole for the cryptococcal antigenaemia (serum CrAg 1:4 with CSF CrAg negative), which was not treated during this admission: 800 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 400 mg daily for 8 weeks, then 200 mg daily maintenance (WHO 2022), with the dose adjusted to renal function.

Resume antiretroviral therapy as soon as oral intake allows (held for several days for vomiting), with tenofovir disoproxil and lamivudine dosed to creatinine clearance or tenofovir disoproxil replaced while kidney function is impaired.

Treat the severe hyponatraemia (sodium 119 mmol/L) as a contributor to the depressed consciousness: assess volume status and cause, correct cautiously with no more than 8 mmol/L rise in 24 hours because malnutrition raises the risk of osmotic demyelination, and monitor sodium every 4 to 6 hours.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Meningeal signs are insensitive, above all in deep impairment of consciousness, advanced HIV and malnutrition; their absence does not exclude meningitis in a febrile obtunded patient.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; IDSA 2017).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because GCS is 9 and she is severely immunocompromised (advanced HIV, CD4 68) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Healthcare-associated meningitis (hospital day 18, urinary catheter since day 5) is treated empirically with vancomycin plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, meropenem when Gram-negative rods are seen (IDSA 2017); the community-acquired regimen does not apply. The catheter is the source and must be removed or replaced.

Adjunctive dexamethasone is not indicated once Gram-negative bacillary healthcare-associated meningitis is established: it has no established benefit here (IDSA 2017), and with CD4 68, cryptococcal antigenaemia and recently treated tuberculous meningitis it adds risk.

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.

A negative multiplex panel never excludes Gram-negative bacillary meningitis: Proteus and other Enterobacterales except E. coli K1 are not panel targets; Gram stain and culture establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.
The Proteus isolate is resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which explains infection despite co-trimoxazole prophylaxis.
Serum cryptococcal antigenaemia with CD4 below 100 calls for pre-emptive fluconazole and, once neurological symptoms appear, a repeat CSF cryptococcal antigen (WHO 2022).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Both diagnoses are considered in parallel: Gram-negative rods on CSF microscopy demand immediate Gram-negative cover, while AFB stain, Xpert MTB/RIF and mycobacterial culture exclude relapse of tuberculous meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilloedema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: GCS 9 (E2 V2 M5), below 10, and advanced HIV with CD4 68. NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (HIV, hospital-acquired infection); WHO 2025 also excludes hospital-acquired meningitis from its scope, so its imaging criteria are applied by analogy, while IDSA 2017 governs the regimen. Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; IDSA 2017).

patient.history_present_illness: This is a 25-year-old woman with a known history of HIV infection and recently treated tuberculous meningitis who has been hospitalized for the past 18 days for evaluation and management of severe abdominal pain, progressive wasting, and malnutrition. Her antiretroviral therapy consists of tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir, which was initiated approximately two years ago. Her most recent CD4 count, obtained on admission, was 68 cells per cubic millimeter, and her HIV viral load was 137 copies per milliliter, indicating suboptimal viral suppression. During this hospitalization, serum cryptococcal antigen testing returned positive; however, cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen was negative, and the patient had no neurological symptoms at that time. Pre-emptive fluconazole was not started. She was diagnosed with pellagra and started on niacin supplementation. Her oral antiretroviral medications were temporarily held for several days due to persistent nausea and vomiting, and she was managed with intravenous fluids and nutritional support. On the morning of hospital day 18, nursing staff found the patient febrile to 39 degrees Celsius with acute deterioration in mental status. She had been conversant and oriented the evening prior but was now obtunded, opening her eyes only to painful stimuli and vocalizing incomprehensible sounds. She was not following commands. There were no witnessed seizure-like movements, and no new rash was observed. The patient had an indwelling urinary catheter placed on hospital day 5 for monitoring of urine output. Physical examination revealed signs of polyserositis with bilateral small pleural effusions and minimal ascites, but no accessible fluid collections for diagnostic aspiration. There was no erythema or purulence at catheter insertion sites or peripheral intravenous access sites. Notably, despite the severely altered consciousness, classical meningeal signs including nuchal rigidity, Kernig sign, and Brudzinski sign were absent on examination. Her ward weight is 44 kg (height 160 cm).

neurological_exam.additional: No nuchal rigidity on examination. No Kernig or Brudzinski signs elicited. Polyserositis with bilateral small pleural effusions and minimal ascites on physical exam. No skin rash or petechiae. Mild generalized muscle wasting. Evidence of chronic malnutrition. No lymphadenopathy. Indwelling urinary catheter in place.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive to light. No papilledema on bedside fundoscopy. Corneal reflexes present bilaterally. No facial asymmetry noted. Oculocephalic reflex intact. Gag reflex present.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Obtunded. Glasgow Coma Scale 9/15 (E2 V2 M5). Does not open eyes spontaneously; opens briefly to painful stimuli. Vocalizes incomprehensible sounds. Localizes pain with upper extremities. Not oriented to person, place, or time. Unable to follow commands.
